title: Data Control & Transaction Control (DCL/TCL)
relevance: SDE interviews probe DCL/TCL to check whether candidates can secure access and keep concurrent writes from corrupting data.

phases.goal: Establish what DCL and TCL are for, how roles grant access, and what ACID guarantees a transaction must provide.

must_hit.point: DCL manages permissions and access rights so each connection gets exactly the privileges it needs and nothing more.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names DCL as permission/access control for users, app servers, and tools—least privilege, not schema DDL.

must_hit.point: In PostgreSQL a Role can own objects and hold privileges, and may act as a login user or as a group whose permissions others inherit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines role as privilege/ownership entity; distinguishes login user vs group inheritance.

must_hit.point: GRANT issues privileges on an object to a role; REVOKE retracts previously granted privileges.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States GRANT adds rights and REVOKE removes them, optionally with concrete SELECT/INSERT examples.

must_hit.point: ACID means Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (valid state to valid state under constraints), Isolation (no interference from others' uncommitted work), and Durability (committed changes survive crash).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists all four with correct one-line meanings, not just the acronym.

must_hit.point: TCL uses BEGIN to start a transaction, COMMIT to permanently save changes, and ROLLBACK to undo all changes since BEGIN.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK and maps each to start, durable save, or full undo.

probes: What is DCL versus TCL, and what does each ACID letter guarantee for a transaction?

hints.1: Think permissions language versus the commands that start, save, or undo a unit of work.
hints.2: Cover roles/GRANT/REVOKE briefly, then Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability, then BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK.
hints.3: DCL = access rights via roles; TCL = BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK; Atomicity = all-or-nothing, Consistency = constraints hold, Isolation = no seeing others' uncommitted intermediates, Durability = committed data survives crash.

phases.goal: Explain how grants, revoke/cascade, RLS, savepoints, isolation levels, and FOR UPDATE actually behave.

must_hit.point: WITH GRANT OPTION lets the recipient re-grant the privilege; REVOKE GRANT OPTION FOR removes only re-grant ability while keeping the privilege; REVOKE ... CASCADE also revokes privileges that were re-granted downstream.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates GRANT OPTION, revoking only the option, and CASCADE removing junior re-grants.

must_hit.point: CREATE ROLE ... WITH LOGIN creates a user that can connect; NOLOGIN creates a group container; GRANT group TO user assigns inherited privileges; DROP ROLE removes a role.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts LOGIN vs NOLOGIN and membership via GRANT role TO role.

must_hit.point: Standard GRANT filters tables or columns; Row-Level Security filters which rows a user can see, via ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and a policy USING predicate.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says RLS is row filtering beyond table/column GRANT, with policy USING as the mechanism.

must_hit.point: SAVEPOINT creates a checkpoint inside a transaction; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes work after that point without abandoning the whole transaction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes partial rollback to a named savepoint while earlier work can still commit.

must_hit.point: Dirty Read sees uncommitted data that may roll back; Non-Repeatable Read sees a committed row change between two reads; Phantom Read sees new rows appear that match the same query.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines the three phenomena distinctly (uncommitted vs same-row change vs new matching rows).

must_hit.point: Read Uncommitted allows all three phenomena; Read Committed prevents Dirty Reads; Repeatable Read prevents Dirty and Non-Repeatable Reads; Serializable prevents all phenomena by behaving as if transactions ran one-by-one.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps each of the four levels to which phenomena it blocks, ending with Serializable as strictest.

must_hit.point: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows so other transactions cannot modify them until COMMIT; NOWAIT errors instead of waiting; SKIP LOCKED skips already-locked rows.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains row lock until commit, plus NOWAIT fail-fast and SKIP LOCKED skip behavior.

probes: Walk through GRANT OPTION versus CASCADE revoke, then how Read Committed differs from Repeatable Read on the three read phenomena.

hints.1: Separate permission mechanics from concurrency mechanics—grants first, then isolation.
hints.2: Cover WITH GRANT OPTION/CASCADE, RLS vs column grants, savepoints, then Dirty/Non-Repeatable/Phantom mapped to the four levels, then FOR UPDATE variants.
hints.3: WITH GRANT OPTION re-grants; CASCADE revokes downstream; RLS filters rows; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT is partial undo; Dirty=uncommitted, Non-Repeatable=same row changed, Phantom=new rows; levels escalate restrictions; FOR UPDATE locks rows, NOWAIT errors, SKIP LOCKED skips.

phases.goal: Show the accuracy-versus-throughput trade-off when choosing isolation levels versus targeted row locks.

must_hit.point: Higher isolation uses stricter locking to prevent more read phenomena but slows concurrent users; lower levels are faster but allow more anomalies.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the ladder: stricter isolation → fewer phenomena → worse concurrency/performance.

must_hit.point: Read Uncommitted is fastest but offers virtually no integrity; Serializable is slowest with massive lock contention (waits or failures); Read Committed is PostgreSQL's default (fast); Repeatable Read is moderate.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Orders performance Fastest/Fast/Moderate/Slowest with default called out as Read Committed.

must_hit.point: Instead of raising the whole system to Serializable, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE can lock only the rows you need until commit, limiting contention to those rows.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts global Serializable slowdown with targeted FOR UPDATE on specific rows.

must_hit.point: PostgreSQL treats Read Uncommitted identically to Read Committed; its Repeatable Read also prevents Phantom Reads though the SQL standard allows them.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both Postgres-specific behaviors relative to the SQL standard.

probes: When would you raise isolation to Serializable versus using SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, and what does PostgreSQL change about Read Uncommitted and Repeatable Read?

hints.1: Frame it as correctness versus how many concurrent transactions you can keep moving.
hints.2: Compare the four levels' speed/strictness, then selective FOR UPDATE as an alternative to global Serializable, then Postgres quirks.
hints.3: Higher level = fewer anomalies, slower; default Read Committed; Serializable = slowest/contention; FOR UPDATE locks only needed rows; Postgres maps Read Uncommitted to Read Committed and RR also blocks phantoms.

phases.goal: Apply DCL/TCL patterns to secure data and keep multi-step and concurrent updates correct.

must_hit.point: A bank transfer must debit and credit in one transaction so a crash mid-way cannot leave money vanished; on restart an uncommitted transaction is fully reversed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses two-step transfer under BEGIN/COMMIT and atomic rollback if power fails mid-transfer.

must_hit.point: Column-level GRANT (e.g. SELECT on name/email only, not salary columns) and RLS policies (e.g. only rows for the caller's department) limit exposure of sensitive data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives column grants and/or RLS department-style row filtering as security application.

must_hit.point: Under weak isolation, reading Checking then Savings across a concurrent transfer can sum to an impossible total (e.g. Seeing Checking before a transfer and Savings after yields 1100 instead of a true point-in-time 1000).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Retells the non-repeatable-read net-worth double-count failure and why multi-row consistency needs stronger isolation or locking.

must_hit.point: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is used for job queues so workers take unlocked pending rows without waiting and without two workers claiming the same job.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes queue workers selecting pending tasks with SKIP LOCKED to avoid wait and double-processing.

probes: How would you implement a safe account transfer and stop two queue workers from processing the same pending job?

hints.1: One answer is about atomic multi-statement updates; the other is about concurrent workers claiming rows.
hints.2: Wrap debit+credit in BEGIN/COMMIT; for queues combine FOR UPDATE with SKIP LOCKED on pending rows.
hints.3: Transfer: BEGIN, debit A, credit B, COMMIT—crash rolls back uncommitted debit; queue: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so locked jobs are skipped and no two workers take the same row.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Climbing from Read Uncommitted/Read Committed toward Repeatable Read and Serializable prevents more Dirty/Non-Repeatable/Phantom phenomena via stricter locking, but moves performance from fastest/fast toward moderate and slowest with lock contention, waits, or failed transactions.

Serializable forces the whole system toward one-by-one results and heavy contention; FOR UPDATE locks only the rows you read until COMMIT, so you get mutual exclusion where needed without raising global isolation.

tradeoffs.topic: Waiting locks vs NOWAIT / SKIP LOCKED
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Default FOR UPDATE makes others wait; NOWAIT fails immediately so the app can retry; SKIP LOCKED skips locked rows, which suits job queues where workers should grab free work without blocking.

gotchas.trap: Assuming Read Uncommitted in PostgreSQL actually allows dirty reads as the SQL ladder suggests.
gotchas.correction: PostgreSQL safely treats Read Uncommitted identically to Read Committed, so you still only read committed data.

gotchas.trap: Assuming Repeatable Read always allows Phantom Reads because the SQL standard says so.
gotchas.correction: PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read is stronger and actually prevents Phantom Reads as well.

gotchas.trap: Confusing Dirty Read, Non-Repeatable Read, and Phantom Read.
gotchas.correction: Dirty = seeing uncommitted data that may vanish; Non-Repeatable = same row's committed value changes between reads; Phantom = new rows appear matching the same query.

gotchas.trap: Thinking REVOKE GRANT OPTION or a plain REVOKE always clears everything downstream.
gotchas.correction: REVOKE GRANT OPTION FOR removes only re-grant ability while keeping the privilege; to pull privileges from roles that received them via GRANT OPTION, use REVOKE ... CASCADE.

gotchas.trap: Performing a multi-step money move without a transaction.
gotchas.correction: Debit and credit must share one BEGIN/COMMIT unit; otherwise a crash between steps can permanently lose money because only part of the work was applied.

gotchas.trap: Raising isolation to Serializable for a single hot row when a narrower tool would do.
gotchas.correction: Prefer SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on that row (optionally NOWAIT/SKIP LOCKED) so only those rows are locked until COMMIT instead of slowing the entire workload.
